newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa BER says time ripe for interest rate cut.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa BER says time ripe for interest rate cut.

text.p: A South African economic think-tank said on Monday the case for interest rate cuts was stronger than ever before despite the negative impact of the lower gold price on the balance of payments.

The University of Stellenbosch's Bureau for Economic Research (BER) said in its latest economic update a two percentage point fall in the Bank rate and prime overdraft rates were still on the cards in the second half of this year, and the first cut could be made as early as this month.
"A third (cut) is still possible early next year," BER said.
The recent fall in the price of gold was expected to lead to the closure of unprofitable gold mines, which would affect gross domestic product and the current account.

The latter could lead to upwards pressure on interest rates, but BER said it believed that the healthy capital account, coupled with a recovery in non-gold exports, would rule out the need to raise interest rates in the immediate future.
"The cumulative balance of payments impact of a persistently weak gold price could be more significant, though," BER said.

The Bureau remains convinced of the need for interest rate cuts because falling real gross domestic expenditure and the broad-based deterioration of business confidence indicated that the economy was slowing down.
Growth forecasts for 1997 were downgraded to 2.2 percent from the previous estimate of 3.1 percent. Next year's economic growth was seen at 3.4 percent.

The inflation cycle caused by the rand's sharp depreciation in 1996 appeared to have turned the corner, BER said, while inflows on the capital account of the balance of payments had been stronger than expected.

"The hurdle of the July 1 exchange control relaxation furthermore appears to be safely out of the way, although one must not underestimate the vulnerable reserve position, even at present healthier levels, and the possibility of downward financial volatility," BER said.
